case.caseTitle: Contractor worker drowned at an overflowing return-water dam (CB-EX-02 facilitator answer)
case.location: North return-water dam and pump installation
case.personsInvolved: Worker A, contractor (deceased); Worker B, contractor (in the boat, reached the bank, hospitalised); Worker C, contractor (held the line from the bank); contractor owner; engineering manager; control room operator.
case.initialDescription: After heavy rain higher up in the catchment, the north return-water dam rose quickly and overflowed, and the pump installation at the dam was flooded. At the engineering manager's request, the owner of a civils contractor on site took three of his workers to help recover the pumps. Two workers went out on the dam in an old boat while the third held a line from the bank. The boat drifted towards the spillway and the two workers left it to swim to the bank. Worker B reached the bank; Worker A drowned. Police divers recovered his body at about 17:30.
case.refinedDescription: On 14 February at about 15:40, a contract worker (Worker A) drowned in the north return-water dam. Heavy rain in the upper catchment raised the dam level quickly and it overflowed at about 14:30 (presumed); the control room noticed only when the pump installation was flooding (EV-001). The engineering manager asked the owner of a civils contractor on site to help recover the pumps. Two of his workers went out in an old boat that had stood unused behind the pump station for years, while a third held a line from the bank. The current and the wind carried the boat towards the spillway and the line was pulled from the attendant's hands. Both workers left the boat to swim to the bank, without life jackets and in overalls and boots. Worker B reached the bank; Worker A, who could not swim, drowned. Police divers recovered his body at about 17:30 (EV-002). No risk assessment, permit or job plan was made, and there was no rescue equipment at the dam. Times, distances and the wind are not yet confirmed.
case.immediateActionsTaken: Emergency services and police called; dam access closed; all work at the dam stopped; Worker B taken to hospital; family informed through the contractor; scene to be held until the investigation team releases it.
case.notificationsRequired: Fatality: regulator (DMRE Inspector of Mines) notified immediately; police inquest; insurers; contractor's compensation fund.

rootCause.immediateCauses: Worker A, who could not swim, entered deep moving water without a life jacket after leaving a drifting boat, and could not be rescued.

evidence.description: Control room occurrence book: handwritten entries for the dam flooding (about 14:50) and the call to the engineering manager. No dam-level alarm entry.
Police recovery report: body recovered at about 17:30 "near the spillway approach". No measured position.
Six phone photos taken by a security officer about an hour after the event from the dam wall: water over the spillway, the boat caught against debris. No scale; two have no time stamp.
Plant rain gauge daily totals for 12 to 14 February (at the plant, not in the upper catchment).

events.text: Heavy rain falls in the upper catchment of the north return-water dam.
Inflow raises the dam level quickly and the dam overflows at the spillway.
Two contractor workers go out on the dam in an old boat; a third holds a line from the bank.
Boat drifts towards the spillway and the line is pulled from the shore attendant's hands.
Both workers leave the boat and try to swim to the bank.
Worker A goes under and drowns.
Shore attendant raises the alarm; nobody at the dam can reach Worker A.
Police divers recover the body of Worker A.
Control room operator sees the pump installation flooding and calls the engineering manager.
Engineering manager phones the contractor owner and asks him to help recover the pumps.
Contractor owner agrees and takes three of his workers to the dam.
The group takes the old boat from behind the pump station and carries it to the water.

conditions.text: No monitoring of rainfall or inflow in the upper catchment is in place.
The dam procedure has no flood trigger levels or flood actions.
The pump installation sits below the maximum flood level of the dam.
No dam-level alarm reaches the control room before the flooding (no alarm entry in the occurrence book).
There is no rule to stop all work on or near a dam while it overflows.
The manager is under pressure to save the pumps and restore pumping.
The work is outside the contractor's contract scope; no onboarding or competence check is done.
No risk assessment, permit or job plan is made for the task.
None of the group has worked on water or been trained in water safety or rescue.
The boat has not been used or inspected for years and has no owner.
No life jackets, ring buoys or throw lines are at the dam.
The workers wear overalls and safety boots.
A single hand-held line is the only way to control the boat.
Strong current towards the spillway and wind across the dam (not yet measured).
The workers fear being carried over the spillway wall.
The distance to the bank is underestimated (thought to be 15 to 20 m; not surveyed).
Worker A cannot swim.
No water-rescue equipment or trained rescuer at the dam, and no first-aid training for drowning.
The contractor management process is slow, so managers routinely ask contractors on site to do odd jobs outside their scope.
Disused equipment is left on site without an owner or control.
The site emergency plan does not cover water rescue at the dams.
PPE rules do not consider the drowning risk of work on or near water.

contributingFactors.text: The dam overflow was not detected in time: no catchment monitoring, no flood trigger levels, and no level alarm before the pumps flooded.
The engineering manager asked a contractor to recover pumps from an overflowing dam (exceptional decision under pressure).
The contractor accepted work on water outside his scope and experience (routine scope creep).
The work started with no risk assessment, plan or competent supervision.
An old, uninspected boat was used, controlled only by a hand-held line.
No life jackets; the workers wore overalls and boots and Worker A could not swim.
The workers left the boat in panic and misjudged the distance to the bank.
No water-rescue equipment, trained rescuer or drowning first aid at the dam.

rootCauses.text: There is no flood management for the return-water dams: no catchment monitoring, no trigger levels, and a pump installation not designed for the flood level.
rootCauses.taprootSubcategory: Standards, Policies or Admin Controls (SPAC) Needs Improvement

rootCauses.text: There is no rule to stop work near an overflowing dam, and no guidance that people come before equipment in an emergency.
rootCauses.taprootSubcategory: Standards, Policies or Admin Controls (SPAC) Needs Improvement

rootCauses.text: The contractor management process is so slow that managers routinely bypass it, so scope, competence and risk checks are skipped.
There is no quick risk-assessment and planning format for emergency or unplanned work.
Disused equipment is not controlled or removed, and nothing requires an inspection before it is used.
There is no site standard for work on or near water (life jackets, rescue equipment, competence, swimming check).
rootCauses.taprootSubcategory: Standards, Policies or Admin Controls (SPAC) Needs Improvement

rootCauses.text: Nobody is trained in water safety, staying with a boat in distress, water rescue or first aid for drowning.
The site emergency plan does not cover water rescue at the dams.
rootCauses.taprootSubcategory: Standards, Policies or Admin Controls (SPAC) Needs Improvement

keyLearnings.text: Other dams and sumps on site also have no ring buoys, throw lines or signs (found during the walk-down after the event).
The disused-equipment yard behind the pump station holds other plant that nobody owns; a separate review is needed.

correctiveActions.finding: No early warning of inflow from the upper catchment.
correctiveActions.action: Install rainfall and inflow monitoring in the upper catchment with alarms to the control room, and set flood trigger levels with actions in the dam operating procedure.

correctiveActions.finding: Pump installation floods before anyone can act.
correctiveActions.action: Raise or relocate the pump installation above the maximum flood level, or fit it for remote isolation and recovery from the bank.

correctiveActions.finding: Work went ahead on an overflowing dam.
correctiveActions.action: Add a stop-work rule to the dam procedure and the site emergency standard: no person on or near the water while a dam overflows; equipment is recovered only after the level is safe.
Introduce a fast-track contractor approval (same-day) that still checks scope, competence and risk, and report out-of-scope contractor work monthly to the mine manager.
Provide a one-page emergency task risk assessment with a stop point, signed off by the shift supervisor before any unplanned task starts.

correctiveActions.finding: Old boat available and used without inspection.
correctiveActions.action: Remove the old boat from site; register all disused equipment with an owner and either remove it or lock it out of use.

correctiveActions.finding: No standard for work on or near water.
correctiveActions.action: Write a work on or near water standard: approved craft only, life jackets for everyone within 2 m of the water, a rescue plan and equipment at the point of work, and a swimming and competence check.

correctiveActions.finding: No life-saving equipment at the dams.
correctiveActions.action: Install ring buoys with throw lines and life-jacket stations at every dam access point, and add them to the monthly inspection.
Train the people who may work at the dams (including contractors) in water safety, staying with a boat in distress, shore-based rescue and first aid for drowning; refresh every two years.

correctiveActions.finding: Emergency plan does not cover water rescue.
correctiveActions.action: Add water rescue at the dams to the site emergency plan, agree response arrangements with the local rescue service, and test them with a drill.

correctiveActions.finding: The workers did not know to stay with the boat.
correctiveActions.action: Put "stay with the boat, wait for rescue" signs at every launch point and in the work on water standard.

correctiveActions.finding: Pressure to save equipment in an emergency.
correctiveActions.action: Brief all managers and supervisors on the stop-work rule and the "people before equipment" principle, and include it in the emergency standard.

correctiveActions.finding: Other dams and water bodies on site.
correctiveActions.action: Inspect all dams, sumps and ponds for access control, signs and life-saving equipment, and fix gaps.
Offer trauma support to Worker B, Worker C, the contractor owner and the engineering manager, and to the family of Worker A.

evidencePlan.narrative:
On the afternoon of 14 February, after heavy rain higher up in the catchment, the north return-water dam rose fast and started to overflow. As far as I can tell the control room only noticed when the pump installation was already being flooded; I assume there was no warning from upstream. The engineering manager phoned the owner of the civils contractor who was on site for other work and asked him to help get the pumps out. I believe this was a one-off request in the emergency, but contractors here are often asked to do odd jobs outside their scope because the contractor process is slow.

The contractor owner brought three of his workers. Two of them went out in an old aluminium boat that had been lying behind the pump station for years; nobody I spoke to knows when it was last used or checked. The third worker stayed on the bank holding a rope tied to the boat. He says the current and the wind pushed the boat towards the spillway and the rope was pulled out of his hands. The two in the boat probably panicked when they saw they were heading for the overflow wall, and they went into the water to swim to the bank. Worker B made it to the bank; Worker A could not swim and drowned. I think they misjudged the distance to the bank, which looks like 15 to 20 m, and their overalls and safety boots would have dragged them down. Worker B was taken to hospital and has not been interviewed yet. There were no life jackets, ring buoys or throw lines at the dam. Nobody did a risk assessment or planned the job, and as far as we know none of them had any training for working on water, rescue or first aid for drowning.

What we do not have yet: drawings of the dam with depths and levels, the spillway height, the positions of the boat and the people, the time line of the alarm and the phone calls, and the wind direction and speed at the time.
evidencePlan.notes: The scene changes fast once the dam level drops: survey the water line, the debris line and the boat position first. Secure the control room level records, phone records and any CCTV today. Interview Worker B, the shore attendant, the contractor owner and the engineering manager separately and as soon as possible, and fix the time line before anything else.

items.item: Interview Worker B, the survivor (separately, as soon as medically fit, with support available)
items.purpose: The only person who was in the boat: why they left it, what they could see, how he reached the bank

items.item: Interview Worker C, the shore attendant (separately, as soon as fit)
items.purpose: Eyewitness from the bank to the drift and to the workers leaving the boat

items.item: Interview the contractor owner
items.purpose: What was asked, what he agreed to, how the boat was chosen, what briefing he gave

items.item: Interview the engineering manager
items.purpose: Why the request was made, what alternatives were considered, who else knew

items.item: Interview the control room operator(s) on shift
items.purpose: When the rising level and the flooding were first noticed and reported

items.item: Interview the recovery and emergency team and the first responders
items.purpose: Response times, rescue equipment available, first aid given

items.item: Post-mortem results and medical reports
items.purpose: Confirms the cause of death and any other factors

items.item: Training records of the contractor owner and the three workers: water safety, rescue, first aid, swimming ability
items.purpose: Tests the account that nobody was trained or could swim

items.item: Surveyed plan and cross-section of the dam: depths, water levels, spillway crest height, pump station and the bank where the line was held
items.purpose: There are no drawings or measurements yet; needed for distances and the drift path

items.item: Flood debris line and high-water marks around the dam, spillway and pump station
items.purpose: Fixes the peak level; disappears as the water drops

items.item: Positions where the boat was launched and found, where the line was held, where Worker B came ashore and where Worker A was recovered, with distances
items.purpose: Reconstructs the drift path and the swim distance (assumed 15 to 20 m)

items.item: Wind direction and speed, and the flow at the spillway at the time
items.source: Site weather station; weather service; pump records
items.purpose: Tests the account that current and wind pushed the boat

items.item: Rainfall data for the upper catchment for the 24 hours before (weather service, upstream gauges)
items.purpose: Tests the assumption that no upstream warning was available

items.item: Photos or videos taken by anyone on site during the event, on phones
items.purpose: May show positions, conditions and wind

items.item: The boat: quarantine it; record condition, leaks, oars or motor, capacity plate, rope attachment point
items.purpose: Was the boat fit for use? Was it ever inspected?

items.item: The rope or line used from the bank: length, type, condition, how it was held or tied
items.purpose: Tests whether the shore control could ever have held the boat

items.item: Clothing, boots and PPE worn by both workers in the boat
items.purpose: Tests the account that clothing and boots hampered swimming; compare survivor and deceased

items.item: Any life jackets, ring buoys or throw lines anywhere on site, and where they are kept
items.purpose: Was life-saving equipment available at all?

items.item: Dam level, pump and alarm logs (SCADA / telemetry) for the day
items.purpose: Time line: when the level rose and when the alarm (if any) went off

items.item: Phone and radio records of the calls between the control room, the engineering manager and the contractor owner
items.purpose: Time line of the request and the response

items.item: CCTV covering the dam, pump station or access road
items.purpose: Independent record of the drift and the time line

items.item: Dam operating manual or procedure, including flood trigger levels and the emergency plan for the dam
items.purpose: Was a flood response defined?

items.item: Any risk assessment, permit or job plan for the task, and the site rule for work on or near water
items.purpose: Confirms that no pre-task risk assessment was done; was work on water controlled?

items.item: Site emergency plan: does it cover water rescue at the dams?
items.purpose: Was rescue from the water planned and resourced?

items.item: Contract, scope of work, site appointment and induction records of the contractor and the three workers
items.purpose: Tests scope creep: was this work within the contract?

items.item: Records of other jobs asked of contractors outside their scope in the last 12 months
items.source: Contractor management office; purchase orders; job cards
items.purpose: Tests the belief that scope creep is routine

items.item: Contractor management procedure and how long onboarding and approval normally take
items.purpose: Tests "the contractor process is slow"

items.item: Asset or stores records for the old boat: when it came to site, last use, any inspection, who owns it
items.purpose: Why was an unused boat available for use?

items.item: Previous incidents, near misses or audit findings for the dams, the pump station or work on water
items.purpose: Was the risk known before?
